Eggs of the European turtle dove, incubated under controlled laboratory conditions at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], hatch after a period of 13.5 days [ab = 13.5 days], an incubation duration that is typical for a columbid of this body size and is tightly linked to the thermal regime experienced by the developing embryo. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge at a remarkably low initial wet weight of 8.2 grams [Ww0 = 8.2 grams], a value reflecting their extreme dependency on parental provisioning for thermoregulation and nutrition. This modest neonatal mass contrasts sharply with the considerable somatic growth that must occur before the young bird can achieve independence, a trajectory that unfolds under the sustained care of both parents throughout the subsequent weeks of development.

Adult body mass in this species exhibits clear sexual size dimorphism, with females reaching a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 142 grams [Wwi = 142 grams] compared to males, which attain an ultimate wet weight of 131 grams [Wwi = 131 grams]. This disparity is a common pattern among many bird species and may be linked to the energetic demands of egg production and the reproductive investment required of the female. Under the consistently warm conditions typical of an active metabolic state, maintained at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the resting metabolic rate of this species reaches a maximum of 205 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 205 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that provides a baseline for understanding the energetic costs of daily existence in a bird of moderate size.

The timing of key developmental milestones in the nestling phase is tightly constrained. Under the same thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the time from hatching until a chick achieves its first sustained flight, known as the fledging period, is approximately 18 days [tx = approximately 18 days]. This relatively rapid development is characteristic of many columbids, whose altricial young are fed a rich, proteinaceous crop milk that facilitates swift somatic growth. Following fledging, the young dove enters a period of gonadal maturation, and the onset of puberty occurs at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching], again at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], indicating that the physiological machinery for reproduction is in place well before the bird typically engages in its first breeding attempt.

The transition to becoming a breeding adult is not immediate after reaching puberty. The time since birth at which a European turtle dove initiates its first successful brood is considerably delayed, occurring at 401.5 days after hatching [tR = 401.5 days after hatching], a value documented under stable conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This significant lag between puberty and first reproduction is often attributed to the need for young birds to acquire a territory, establish a pair bond, and accumulate sufficient body condition to support the energetic costs of egg production and incubation. In terms of the maximum reproductive rate, field studies have shown that females typically lay exactly 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], a highly consistent clutch size across the family Columbidae. Furthermore, they average 2.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2.5 clutches per year] under favorable conditions at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], allowing for multiple nesting attempts within a single breeding season to compensate for potential predation or failure.

The maximum lifespan documented for this species, measured under field conditions approximating an average body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], is 4343.5 days [am = 4343.5 days]. When converted to more conventional terms, this longevity is equivalent to just under 12 years, a respectable duration for a small to medium-sized bird and one that allows for multiple reproductive seasons across a lifetime. This extended lifespan, combined with the moderate clutch size and the capacity for several nesting attempts per year through a high clutch frequency [F_R_i = several nesting attempts per year through a high clutch frequency], suggests a life-history strategy that balances adult survival against periodic reproductive output. Comparative data from related species within the genus Streptopelia indicate that such longevity is not unusual, and it likely reflects an evolutionary response to the variable environmental conditions encountered across its migratory range, where a longer life permits multiple opportunities for successful recruitment.
